newsitem.title: UK: UK, US insurers seen prospering in Indian market.
newsitem.headline: UK, US insurers seen prospering in Indian market.

text.p: UK and U.S. companies are most likely to benefit from the expected liberalisation of the Indian insurance market, M.V. Purohit, chairman of the Oriental Insurance Company Ltd, told an industry seminar.

"There will be more players, joint ventures, mostly UK and U.S. companies and one or two Japanese, maybe a dozen or more altogether," he said at a seminar organised by the Insurance Institute of London.

The timetable for the privatisation of the currently nationalised Indian insurance sector was uncertain, Purohit said, but legislation was likely next year, with February being the earliest possible month.

India represents a potentially huge market for insurers, Purohit said, with a middle class estimated at some 230 million people and growth in sales of insurance outstripping gross national product expansion.
"I have no doubt that this country is poised for very, very strong growth in the next ten years," he told his London insurance market audience.

The non-life insurance market would easily support up to two dozen local and foreign insurance companies, Purohit added. Local insurers were gearing up for change and gradually introducing computerisation.
Oriental is one of four companies owned by the General Insurance Corporation (GIC) set up in 1973 when the non-life insurance industry was nationalised.
The other three are National Insurance Company Limited, The New India Assurance Company Limited and United India Insurance Company Limited.
The GIC replaced 107 insurers which existed before privatisation, including 27 from the UK, three from the U.S., three from Switzerland and two from Germany.
Gross direct premium in the Indian market was $1.683 billion in 1995/96 compared with $52.66 million in 1973.
